questions.q: Which isolation level allows dirty reads and is what the NOLOCK table hint simulates?
questions.explain: READ UNCOMMITTED takes minimal locks and can read uncommitted data from other transactions — a dirty read.

questions.q: What makes SERIALIZABLE the strictest isolation level?
options: It holds range locks so no other transaction can insert new rows into the range a query touched
It only applies to SELECT statements
questions.explain: SERIALIZABLE locks the range a query touched, preventing phantom reads by blocking inserts into that range too.

questions.q: What do SNAPSHOT isolation and RCSI use instead of locks to prevent readers and writers from blocking each other?
options: Row versioning via tempdb's version store
questions.explain: Both use tempdb's version store to give readers a consistent snapshot instead of taking locks against writers.

questions.q: What's the key practical difference between turning on RCSI versus using SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SNAPSHOT?
options: RCSI changes the default behavior of READ COMMITTED for all sessions with no code changes; SNAPSHOT must be explicitly opted into per transaction
They are functionally identical in every way
RCSI only works in tempdb, never in user databases
SNAPSHOT isolation cannot be enabled at the database level
questions.explain: RCSI is a database-level default switch; full SNAPSHOT isolation requires each transaction to explicitly request it.

questions.q: In sys.dm_exec_sessions, what does a transaction_isolation_level value of 2 represent?
questions.explain: The numeric mapping is 1=READ UNCOMMITTED, 2=READ COMMITTED, 3=REPEATABLE READ, 4=SERIALIZABLE, 5=SNAPSHOT.
